A Harvard working paper finds coding agents raised code output while review time rose 49%. Why verification, not generation, should decide whether an agent is useful.
Archive

An agent with a shell, a file system and network access is only useful if you can trust what it will do with them. A tour of the layers between the model and your machine: scopes, approvals, a blocklist nothing can override, an SSRF guard, and tiers for unattended bots.
The team behind Mercury. Postmortems, design notes and the reasoning behind how Mercury works.
Founder, Cosmic Stack. Builds Mercury. Writes about agent runtimes, terminal UIs and shipping open source.
One background runtime that every terminal attaches to, bots that deliver real files and stay online, and a fleet you can run from Telegram. What changed in the 1.3 line and why.
Always-on agents shipped everywhere this autumn. How Mercury Bots work, what we measured, how they compare with Grok Bot, OpenAI dots, Meta Muse, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, and the commits behind it.
We read Mercury's scheduler and budget code and reproduced one behaviour, to find what fails during long unattended runs: skipped tasks, quiet errors, overlapping jobs and budget stops.

For six releases, a brand-new Mercury install asked for your name, showed one menu, and exited without an error. A walkthrough of a one-tick race between two readers of the same terminal, and the test that now keeps it from coming back.

Typing felt sluggish on every machine, and the terminal renderer took the blame. The real cause was a second full copy of the agent, started quietly by the launcher. How we found it, and why the fix was an architecture change rather than a performance tweak.

Mercury offers two ways to work on a repository: a CLI workspace (terminal-based IDE with keyboard navigation) and a Web Workspace IDE (full graphical editor in the browser). Both share the same backend tools and Git operations.

Mercury connects to Discord as a bot, providing a real-time conversational interface with slash commands, streaming responses, rich embeds, and an organization-style access model with admin roles and pairing codes.

Mercury can act as your GitHub companion — creating pull requests, reviewing PRs, managing issues, and making co-authored commits — all through natural conversation. When configured, five GitHub tools are registered alongside Mercury's built-in toolset, letting you manage repositories without leaving the terminal or Telegram.

Kanban Boards are a beta feature in v1.1.9. The data model and API surface are stable, but expect UI refinements in subsequent releases. The web dashboard labels this section "Kanban Boards (Beta mode)".
Persistent, persona-scoped agents that run outside your conversation — each with its own persona, sandbox, skills, permission scopes, and durable queue. Build fleets with lead bots and crews.

Mercury connects to Signal via a signal-cli bridge, providing an end-to-end encrypted conversational interface with support for group chats and private DMs, pairing-code access control, and real-time task progress.

Mercury connects to Slack as a Socket Mode bot, providing a real-time conversational interface with slash commands, streaming responses, and an organization-style access model with pairing codes and admin controls.

Mercury connects to your Spotify account natively — control playback, search music, manage playlists, and DJ on your devices through natural conversation. No browser tabs, no app switching. Just say "play some chill music" and Mercury handles the rest.

Mercury isn't just a chatbot — it's an orchestrator. It can spawn parallel AI agents to handle tasks concurrently while continuing the conversation. This is sub-agent mode, and it changes how Mercury works fundamentally.
Mercury connects to Telegram via a bot token, providing a mobile-first interface with streaming, file uploads, inline approval keyboards, and real-time task progress.
Mercury Web is a React single-page application that provides a visual interface for managing every part of the agent — chat, memory, tasks, code, and configuration. It runs locally at http6174.
Mercury has a built-in toolset it can use during conversations. These are not CLI commands — the agent decides when to call them.
How Mercury Code guarantees honest, verified, stall-free task completions — the completion contract, the escalation harness, and the recovery map.
All runtime data lives in ~/.mercury/ — not in your project directory.
Mercury has a layered permission system that controls what actions the agent can take. The behavior differs significantly between Ask Me and Allow All modes.
Configure multiple LLM providers. Mercury tries them in order and falls back automatically. When a provider fails, Mercury tries the next one and remembers the last successful provider.
Mercury can schedule tasks using cron expressions or one-shot delays.

Mercury has a persistent, structured memory that grows with every conversation. When enabled, it automatically extracts, stores, and retrieves facts about you — your preferences, goals, projects, habits, the people in your life, and the relationships between them.
Skills are Markdown-based extensions that teach Mercury how to do a specific task. Each skill is a single SKILL.md file in ~/.mercury/skills// and follows the Agent Skills specification.

Token Saver Mode is a battery-saver-style optimization layer for LLM calls. When active, Mercury produces shorter, terser responses, runs fewer reasoning steps, and uses a smaller history window — saving tokens at the cost of some verbosity and exploration depth.
Mercury Agent release notes — what shipped, when, and why.
Mercury becomes a skillful platform. Skill System, Token Saver Mode, standalone binaries on five OS targets, redesigned bottom status bar with per-step spinners, and a new built-in screenshot skill.
Hotfix on top of v1.1.11. Standalone binaries can now start in the background, so Telegram works again for users who installed Mercury via the one-line installer.

Mercury gets chatty. Three new channels — Discord, Slack, and Signal — bring Mercury to where you already are, with end-to-end encryption, organization access models, and real-time streaming. Plus long-running loop fixes, CLI heartbeat improvements, and crash recovery.
Release 1.1.6 focuses on a major CLI/TUI upgrade, workspace IDE flow, background execution reliability, and docs coverage.

Release 1.1.7 brings two new providers (ChatGPT Web and GitHub Copilot), a redesigned real-time progress system, Mercury Autopilot with intelligent loop detection, major Telegram improvements, and a full landing page redesign with the interactive Killipi mascot.

Release 1.1.9 introduces the Mercury Web Dashboard — a full React SPA at localhost:6174 — alongside a persistent Kanban board system, an in-browser Workspace IDE with Git and AI commit messages, a dual-layer (conscious + subconscious) Second Brain, intelligent skill batching, and a cross-platform build pipeline.

documents.t: Mercury meets the cloud. Terminal pairing, JWT auth with self-recovery, Cloud WebSocket for real-time remote control, shared memory pool search, and cross-platform fixes for Windows and Termux. Patch set 1.2.0 → 1.2.1 → 1.2.2.

The release where Mercury Code stops dying and starts telling the truth. Completion contract, AUTO mode, the escalation harness, compact-on-pressure, live plan checklist, and security hardening across the tool surface.

Mercury stops being one agent and becomes a fleet. Persistent persona-scoped bots with private sandboxes, durable queues, multi-level fleets with self-organizing leads, bundles, a web cockpit, and honest observability.

One process runs the fleet and your channels; the terminal attaches to it instantly. Bots do real work, deliver files you can find, stay online without burning tokens, and run from your phone. Node 22, patched Ink 8, and the whole unpublished 1.3.1 line.

Lines generated, commits, and pull request count are easy to count, and in the study they all went up. None of them shows whether the work is finished. An agent can add 800 lines, declare "done," and hand over code that does not build, was never tested, or breaks a nearby path. Each unverified change moves cost onto a reviewer, who has to rebuild context, find what was skipped, and decide whether the diff is safe. Review burden is a fair metric, but it needs care. More comments on a large change do not automatically mean worse code. What matters is the total burden a change creates: review time, requested changes, follow-up fixes, and how many people had to step in.

Did it verify its work? Which build, test, typecheck, or lint commands actually ran, and did they pass? "This should work" is not verification. How much review burden did it create? Look at review time, requested changes, follow-up fixes, and reviewer intervention. Did it catch failures before handing back? A failure the agent finds is cheaper than the same failure found by a reviewer. Did it satisfy the task, or only produce valid code? Code can compile and pass tests while still missing the requirement. Compiling is not correctness. Passing tests is not the requirement being met. The fourth question is the one most dashboards miss.
documents.s: Better questions for a coding agent

documents.t: Verification and human review overlap, but they are not the same thing. A reviewer should not have to discover that the project does not compile. A coding agent should handle: build checks tests type checking linting obvious runtime failures Human reviewers should spend their time on: architecture and maintainability security product requirements edge cases that automated checks cannot see The goal is not to remove human review. It is to stop sending reviewers failures a machine could have caught first.

Checks can be made meaningless. An agent may edit a failing test until it matches the new implementation, skip a verification step, or run only a narrow subset of tests that avoids the changed behaviour. The result is a green run that gives false confidence. No intent is needed for this to happen. The check simply stops testing what it claims to test. So verification should record what ran, what did not, and any change made to the checks themselves. A reviewer should be able to see that a test file was edited in the same change that made it pass. Passing checks can also be too narrow. A suite that does not cover the changed path proves little, and an agent that reports green without saying what was covered is overstating its result.
documents.s: Why verification is hard to get right

documents.t: Mercury Code treats completion as something that needs evidence. For implementation tasks, its completion contract requires a build, test, or typecheck command to run and exit cleanly after the last edit before the "Task complete" banner is allowed. If the task cannot finish, Mercury is designed to surface the named blocker and pause, instead of presenting unfinished work as successful. The completion architecture describes the details. That does not replace human code review. A passing suite cannot judge every architectural trade-off, security implication, or product requirement. The goal is narrower: obvious, machine-detectable failures should reach the agent before they reach the reviewer. For any coding agent, including Mercury, ask for three things with each change: The exact commands run and their results. The parts of the change that were not verified. Any blocker that stopped the task from finishing. If an agent cannot give you those, it has produced code, not finished work.

Primary (working paper, not yet peer-reviewed) Fiona Chen and James Stratton, Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production, Harvard University, job-market paper, August 2026. fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf Secondary Ars Technica, coverage of the same study. arstechnica.com

The model never decides what it's allowed to do. It can ask to run npm test or write a file, but the decision happens in ordinary code, outside the model, before anything touches your machine. Prompt injection can change what the model asks for. It can't change the code that answers. Everything below is that code.

Some commands are never run, no matter which mode you're in, who's asking or what you approved earlier. sudo is one. Recursive deletes of the root or home directory are another, in every spelling we've seen: rm -rf /, rm -fr ~, rm -rf /*, and their PowerShell equivalents like Remove-Item -Recurse -Force C:\ with the flags in any order. The list is matched against each segment of a command. Mercury splits pipelines, chains and command substitutions apart first, and anything it can't fully decompose is treated as needing approval, so wrapping a blocked command in $( ) or chaining it after && doesn't hide it. It's deliberately short. A blocklist can't make an agent safe on its own. What it can do is make sure the handful of truly unrecoverable commands are off the table even in the most permissive configuration.
documents.s: Layer 1: a blocklist nothing can override

documents.t: File access is scoped to folders, and each scope is either read-only or read-write. Out of the box Mercury can read and write in the directory it's working in, and nothing else. If a task needs another folder, Mercury asks, and you can grant it for that one request or permanently. A short list of read-only commands runs without a prompt, because asking every time someone types ls trains people to click Allow without reading: things like ls, cat, pwd, git status, git diff and git log, plus npm test and npm run. Scopes apply to shell commands too. If a command writes to a path outside your granted scopes, Mercury treats it the same as a file write outside them. Scopes are per channel and per role. If you share a Telegram group with Mercury in it, members can talk to the agent, but they can't install skills or widen what it's allowed to touch. Those decisions stay with admins.

When something isn't covered by a scope, Mercury asks. In the terminal you get an arrow-key prompt. On Telegram you get buttons. In the web dashboard you get a card with Allow, Always allow and Deny. The prompt says exactly what will happen: the command, the file path, the folder being requested. You choose the default per session: Ask Me prompts for every write and every command outside your scopes. Even when a scope already covers a folder, writes in Ask Me mode still prompt. Allow All runs without prompting, inside the blocklist. One detail we're careful about: Allow All applies to the session where you turned it on. A request that arrives from a different channel doesn't inherit your permissive setting. If you said "allow all" in your terminal, a message from a Telegram group is still checked as a Telegram message.

fetch_url is how Mercury reads the web, and it's a classic way to attack a self-hosted service: ask the agent to fetch http://192.168.1.1/admin, or a public URL that redirects to one, and it becomes a proxy into your home network. So every fetch is checked before it connects: Only http and https. The hostname is resolved, and if any address in the answer is private, loopback or link-local, the request is refused. A resolver that returns one public and one private address doesn't get the benefit of the doubt. The connection is pinned to the address that was checked. A hostile DNS server can't hand Mercury a public address for the check and a private one for the actual request. Redirects are followed manually and each hop is checked again, up to five. Responses are also size-capped, so a page can't flood the model's context.

Mercury Bots run unattended. A bot working at 3 a.m. has nobody to ask, so for bots the rule flips: anything not explicitly granted is denied. A missing permission isn't a question, it's a no. When you create a bot you pick a tier: Tier What it can do Read-only (the default) Browse, search, read files, message other bots. No commands, no writes. Builder Also create and edit files inside its granted folders. Still no shell. Operator Also run commands, restricted to its granted folders. The blocklist still applies. Full access Everything, including deleting files. Meant for automation you fully trust. Each bot also has its own folder scopes, its own daily token budget, and its own memory. A bot's tier is a ceiling: a crew member can't do more than the permissions it was given, regardless of what its lead asks it to do.

API keys live in ~/.mercury/.env, not in the main config file, and the logger redacts anything that looks like a key or token before it's written. The web dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1 only, and its first password is randomly generated and shown once, so there's no default credential from the public source code that works on every install.
documents.s: Layer 6: secrets stay out of the conversation

documents.t: It's worth being direct about the limits. If you choose Allow All and give Mercury write access to your home folder, it can do a lot of damage inside the blocklist, because you told it it could. Skills from the community registry are not audited, and a skill's instructions become part of what the model reads, so review them before installing. And no permission system makes a model's judgement correct. Mercury can still decide to do the wrong thing. The permission layers decide whether it's allowed to, and give you the chance to say no.

documents.s: Mercury 1.3: an agent you can actually leave running

documents.t: Until 1.3, typing mercury in a terminal could start a full copy of the agent in that terminal, even when a background copy was already running. That sounds harmless. It wasn't. Two copies meant two Telegram pollers fighting over one bot token, two schedulers firing the same routines, and bot work running on the same thread that draws your keystrokes. We wrote up the details in We were running Mercury twice and didn't know it. Now there is exactly one process that owns your channels, your bots and the web dashboard. It runs as a login service on macOS, Linux and Windows. When you type mercury, the terminal attaches to that process. Close the terminal and nothing stops. Open it again and you're back in under a second. Two smaller changes make this hold up in practice: The login service follows the install. If you move from npm to the standalone binary, or from stable to the dev channel, Mercury notices that the service still points at the old install and re-points it. Before this, an old daemon could keep resurrecting itself on every login and hold the web port. Lag is now a number. /api/health reports how long the event loop has stalled in the last ten seconds, and stalls over 250 ms are logged. "It feels slow" turns into something we can actually look at.
documents.s: One runtime, and the terminal is just a window

documents.t: Mercury Bots shipped in 1.3.0. After a couple of weeks of running a real fleet we looked at the journals and didn't love what we saw: routines that produced status notes about other status notes, turns that read 750,000 tokens of context to decide nothing needed doing, and finished output buried somewhere under ~/.mercury. So 1.3 judges a bot run by what it did, not by what it said. Every run gets an outcome computed from the tool trace: it delivered a file, it took an action, it delegated, it replied, or it did nothing. A scheduled routine that does nothing three times in a row cools down for a few hours and then resumes by itself. Bots stay online. They just stop burning tokens on busywork. Finished work goes somewhere you can find it: ~/Documents/Mercury/<Bot name>/, with final results at the top and work in progress under work/. There's a daily token budget per bot (5M by default) and per fleet, with a warning at 80%. Fleets got real coordination too. A lead bot can hand typed tasks to several crew members at once and gets woken up once, with a summary, when they're all done. A lead's standard job can be written down as a pipeline in bot.yaml, so "research, draft, fact-check, package" runs without the lead having to babysit each step.
documents.s: Bots that do work instead of writing about work

documents.t: A lot of you run Mercury on a home server and talk to it from Telegram, so 1.3 makes Telegram a first-class control surface. /bots shows the roster with Stop, Start and Run buttons for each bot. When a bot finishes a task you asked for from your phone, the result arrives as an attached file, not a path on a machine you can't see. You can create a bot from Telegram too: describe its persona in a message, then pick its permissions, whether it works alone or leads a crew, and its budget, all with buttons.

The npm package now requires Node.js 22. The standalone binaries carry their own runtime, so if you installed with the one-line installer, nothing changes for you. If you're on npm, mercury upgrade checks your Node version before it touches anything, and the package refuses to install on an older Node with a readable message instead of installing something that won't start. We also moved the terminal UI to Ink 8 with four patches of our own. The most visible one fixes a problem where long replies stamped copies of themselves into your scrollback on every repaint. The patches live in a public fork and we're working on getting them upstream.
documents.s: Node 22 and a patched terminal renderer

documents.t: The 1.3 line had more point releases than we'd like, from 1.3.2 to 1.3.8 in three days. Each one fixed something real: the first-run setup could quit at its first menu, /code didn't work from the default launch, the Windows installer failed on stock PowerShell 5.1, and the Linux binary crashed on CPUs without AVX2. The Windows and AVX2 reports came from people who took the time to dig in and tell us exactly what they saw. Thank you. Every one of those now has a test that would have caught it: the setup wizard runs under a real pseudo-terminal in CI, the Windows installer runs under PowerShell 5.1, and the Linux installer is tested on a CPU that pretends to lack AVX2.

A bot is a folder. Each one lives at ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/ and holds four files: bot.yaml sets its identity, model, schedules and fleet position. persona.md holds its character and standing instructions. permissions.yaml is the only file that decides what it may touch. .env holds credentials that only this bot can read. Bots form fleets. A lead bot owns a goal and has a crew of specialists, and crews can have their own crews. A typical fleet is a lead that plans a weekly report, a researcher, a writer and a fact-checker. Each one can run on a different model from a different provider, because the model is a per-bot setting. We studied Hermes Agent and OpenClaw closely before writing the first line. Our design notes credit both, and you can read them in BOTS-ARCHITECTURE.md. The first runtime landed on September 16: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent69417f0 feat(bots): P0 — persistent persona-scoped bot runtime Implements the Mercury Bots P0 milestone per BOTS-ARCHITECTURE.md and ADR-012: multiple persistent persona-scoped agents (own character, model, scoped memory, tool permissions) running as in-process coroutines that never touch Agent.processQueue, fail-closed and near-zero-intera… hotheadhacker committed Sep 16, 202617 files changed+2.7K −1 src/bots/bot-manager.ts+506 −0 src/bots/bot-manager.test.ts+359 −0 BOTS-ARCHITECTURE.md+334 −0 src/bots/store.ts+315 −0 src/bots/store.test.ts+263 −0

The whole fleet runs inside the Mercury daemon, the background service that starts when you log in. There is no process per bot and no thread per bot. A bot turn is asynchronous work in the same Node.js process, scheduled through one lane with a concurrency cap. That choice comes from the hardware our users run Mercury on: a Raspberry Pi, a small VPS, or a phone under Termux. A separate Node.js process costs tens of megabytes before it does anything, and a fleet of fifteen bots should not need fifteen of them. FlowchartOne process, many botsCopy sourceExpand Everything here runs inside the Mercury daemon on your machine. The terminal, the web dashboard and Telegram only attach to it. Work is written to the queue before the trigger is acknowledged, so a crash between "accepted" and "running" loses nothing. Jobs are claimed on a lease. If the daemon dies mid-turn, the lease expires and the job runs again. Failures are typed. A provider timeout is retried with backoff, and a permission denial goes straight to a dead-letter queue you can inspect and replay. The queue uses SQLite when the platform has it and falls back to a JSON file store when it doesn't, so it works on the same devices as the rest of Mercury. We learned the hard way that "one process" has to mean exactly one. Until a fix earlier this month, the launcher could start a second full copy of the runtime, and both copies ran the fleet. We wrote that story up in We were running Mercury twice and didn't know it.

An agent that runs at 3 a.m. can't wait for you to tap "Allow". Most products in this space solve that with approval prompts that time out, or with a second model that reviews actions. We chose a stricter rule. A bot has no ask handler at all. Anything granted in its permissions.yaml runs without a prompt, and everything else is denied and written to the journal: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent@ 705f6c0View on GitHub ↗ src/bots/registry-factory.ts · L114–123 // Fail-closed core: no ask handler, no allow-all, non-internal context. // Granted scopes apply without prompting; everything else denies. pm.setAutoApproveAll(false); pm.setFailClosed(true); pm.setCurrentContext('bot', deps.botId); // Relative paths and shell commands resolve inside the bot's workspace, // never the daemon's cwd (a bot with a wide grant wrote "sandbox/…" files // into whatever repo the daemon happened to be started from). registry.setCwd(deps.sandbox?.workspace ?? process.cwd()); At 705f6c0 · feat(bots): budgets by default, routine gate, 3-strike pause, visible deliverables (ADR-020) · Oct 10, 2026 Three details matter here: No allow-all for bots. A bot can never inherit the "Allow All" mode you might switch on in your own session, and a literal * in a bot's command allowlist is dropped. The deny list wins. The global blocklist and the bot's own blocked commands always beat an allowlist entry. The workspace is the default. Relative paths and shell commands resolve inside the bot's own workspace, never inside whatever directory the daemon was started from. We added that after a bot with a wide grant wrote its sandbox files into a real repository. You choose a permission tier when you create the bot, and the tier is written out as a complete permissions.yaml. If a bot keeps getting denied, the journal shows you exactly which action was refused, and you widen the grant on purpose.

It reads the tool trace of the run and decides: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent@ fad01f2View on GitHub ↗ src/bots/bot-turn.ts · L639–657 export function computeOutcome(input: { trace: BotToolTraceEntry[]; deliveries: string[]; expects: BotExpectedOutcome; text: string; sandbox: { workspace: string; shared: string }; }): BotOutcome { if (input.deliveries.length > 0) return 'deliverable'; const roots = [input.sandbox.workspace, input.sandbox.shared]; for (const t of input.trace) { if (!t.ok) continue; if (ACTION_TOOLS.has(t.name)) return 'action'; if (FILE_WRITE_TOOLS.has(t.name) && t.arg && !insideAny(t.arg, roots)) return 'action'; if (t.name === 'run_command' && t.arg && !isReadOnlyCommand(t.arg)) return 'action'; } if (input.trace.some((t) => t.ok && t.name === 'bot_send' && t.task)) return 'delegated'; if (input.expects === 'message' && input.text.trim().length > 0) return 'message'; return 'none'; } At fad01f2 · feat(bots): typed tasks with fan-in, pipelines as data, continuity and memory (ADR-021) · Oct 10, 2026 A run produced a deliverable if it handed over a finished file, or an action if it changed something outside its own sandbox or ran a command that isn't read-only. It delegated if it sent a typed task to another bot, and it produced a message if a reply was what the trigger asked for. Anything else is none. Writing notes into its own sandbox doesn't count, and the journal flags any reply that claims work the trace doesn't show. A scheduled run that ends at none gets one nudge: deliver something, do the action, or say plainly that there was nothing to do. If a routine comes back empty three times in a row, it cools down for six hours, then twelve, up to a day, and then resumes by itself. Date.parse(pausedEntry.until) : Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY; if (Date.now() < until) return { jobId: '', accepted: false, reasonCode: 'routine_paused' }; // Cooldown over: the routine is live again with a clean streak (liveness contract). delete routineState.paused[key]; delete routineState.noOutcomeStreak[key]; this.store.writeRoutineState(botId, routineState); logger.info({ botId, routineKey: key }, 'Bot routine cooldown over — resuming'); } if (queue.length > 0 || (this.running.get(botId)?.size ?? 0) > 0) return { jobId: '', accepted: false, reasonCode: 'busy' }; const lastEnd = this.routineLastEnd.get(key); const minGapMs = this.routineConfig(manifest, key).minIntervalMinutes * 60_000; if (lastEnd !== undefined && Date.now() - lastEnd < minGapMs) return { jobId: '', accepted: false, reasonCode: 'too_soon' }; } At 8b2078b · fix(providers): bots always get a provider that works; rejected keys are skipped; doctor flags malformed keys (1.3.3) · Oct 12, 2026 FlowchartThe life of a scheduled routineCopy sourceExpand A tick is an opportunity, not an order. Skipped ticks cost no tokens, and a cooled-down routine resumes by itself. The point is that the bot stays alive. "Always-on" doesn't mean calling a model all day. It means idle between runs, never silently dead, and never spending money to tell you it had nothing to do.

documents.t: When a lead delegated to five crew members, it used to get five free-text emails and run five full turns to read them. Now delegation is data. A task has a goal, acceptance criteria, an assignee, a status and a typed result. Tasks travel in batches with a wake policy and a deadline, and the lead is woken once, with a digest, when the batch is done: SequenceA lead delegates a batch and wakes up onceCopy sourceExpand The crew works in parallel. The lead spends one turn to dispatch and one to synthesise, however many crew members there are. A fleet's standard job can be written down as a pipeline in bot.yaml. Stages chain themselves, each one gets the previous stage's result, and the lead isn't woken between stages at all. A five-member crew now costs the lead one turn to dispatch and one to synthesise. Bots also remember, without writing status files. Every prompt carries the bot's last five journal rows and its own short working note. Honesty cuts both ways, so here is where each of them beats us today. A computer of their own. Grok Bot, dots and Muse give your agents a cloud computer with a real browser they can drive, which you can watch and take over. The work continues with your laptop closed. A Mercury fleet runs where you install it. If that machine sleeps, the fleet sleeps, which is why many of our users run it on a home server or a small VPS. Reach. OpenClaw lists 33 chat channels and Hermes lists more than 20. Our tappable fleet controls exist on Telegram today. Discord and Slack get the same commands as text. Scale. OpenClaw and Hermes have far larger communities, a larger skills ecosystem and many more people finding their edge cases. Consumer polish. Muse pays for things with single-use cards and asks before each purchase. dots connects to a much larger catalogue of apps than we do. Every project in this table is candid about the same unsolved problem. Meta writes that "prompt injection remains an open problem in the industry." The system card for GPT-6 Astra, the model behind dots, reports test runs in which the agent overstepped its authorisation. Hermes Agent's own security policy says that "the only security boundary against an adversarial LLM is the operating system." OpenClaw's skills registry had a wave of malicious uploads in February. Our answer isn't that Mercury is immune. It's that a bot can only do what one file says it may, that it spends inside a budget it can't raise, and that every run leaves a record you can read.

Delayed tasks are saved to schedules.yaml in Mercury's home directory, with an executeAt time. On startup, restorePersistedTasks in src/core/scheduler.ts checks each one. If executeAt has already passed, it logs Delayed task already expired, skipping and does not run it. For example, a delayed task due at 02:40, during a restart at 02:50, will not fire. A task due at 03:00 during the same restart will. Cron tasks are re-registered on startup. We found no catch-up logic in the scheduler, so firings that fall inside a downtime window are not replayed. Different features behave differently; bot routines go through their own governor, described below. What to do: Use cron for recurring work. For one-off work that must run, check the log for already expired after every restart.
documents.s: Delayed tasks due during downtime are skipped [Confirmed from code]

documents.t: This claim is narrow. The scheduler's own error handlers only log: In addTask, a throwing handler logs Scheduled task error. Nothing else happens. In startHeartbeat, a failing heartbeat logs Heartbeat error. In addDelayedTask, a failing delayed task logs Delayed task error. Ordinary scheduled prompts take a different route. handleScheduledTask in src/core/agent.ts catches its own errors and logs Scheduled task execution failed. So for ordinary tasks, the scheduler's Scheduled task error path is usually not the one that fires. It fires for bot routines, where an error from enqueueing is not caught. Successful output is separate. A scheduled task's result goes back through its source channel like any other reply. We did not check whether a failure inside the agent loop is sent to the channel, so treat a missing result as unknown, not as success. What to do: Don't rely on error logs for overnight work. Have each task send a short end-of-run message. If it doesn't arrive, assume the run did not finish.
documents.s: Some scheduler errors are logged but not sent to you [Confirmed from code]

documents.t: In addDelayedTask, a finally block removes the task from schedules.yaml when its handler returns, even if the handler threw. For ordinary tasks, handleScheduledTask does not throw, so the removal happens once the prompt has been queued. The queued prompt is not lost on that basis alone. Accepted jobs are persisted in the work ledger, and on startup recoverInterrupted() re-queues the ones that were queued or interrupted (src/core/agent.ts). We have not tested a restart in the middle of a run.
documents.s: A delayed task leaves the schedule file once its prompt is handed off [Confirmed from code]

documents.t: Each cron task is registered with cron.schedule and an async handler. The scheduler keeps no in-flight flag per task ID. We reproduced this pattern with node-cron 3.0.3, the version Mercury pins: a job firing every second, with a handler that takes 3.5 seconds, reached four concurrent runs within eight seconds. Inside Mercury, the effect is different. Scheduled prompts go onto the agent's message queue, which processes one message at a time. Overlapping firings for a main-agent task therefore wait in line rather than running in parallel. [Confirmed from code; not run end to end.] Each queued firing still costs budget when it runs. Bot routines are different. The bot governor skips a tick when the bot is busy or the last run was too recent (busy, too_soon). [Confirmed from code.] What to do: Until overlap is tested on your own setup, avoid non-idempotent jobs (ones that write files, send messages, or spend money) with intervals shorter than their expected run time.
documents.s: Long runs may overlap [Reproduced at the scheduler level; queued inside the agent]

documents.t: Mercury tracks daily token use in src/utils/tokens.ts. The total is saved to token-usage.json and resets when the date changes, so a restart does not reset it. isOverBudget() is checked in handleMessage in src/core/agent.ts, before the agent loop runs. Scheduled prompts are not exempt. They enter the same queue and reach the same check, so a scheduled job is stopped by the same daily budget as chat. What differs is who hears about it: A chat message gets a budget notice. On the CLI, it gets an override prompt. A scheduled job with a source channel gets the same notice on that channel. A scheduled job with no source channel (internal) gets nothing. The check returns without sending a message. We traced this in the code but did not run it: we did not set a one-request budget and fire a job. To confirm on your install, set a low budget, fire one scheduled job with a source channel and one without, and check what each sends and logs. What to do: Keep daily headroom for the overnight run. Give unattended jobs a source channel so the notice reaches you. Check /budget in the morning.
documents.s: Budget stops can be silent for unattended jobs [Confirmed from code]

documents.t: Recurring work is on cron, not one-off delays. Each overnight task sends an end-of-run message. No message means unknown. Non-idempotent jobs don't run on intervals shorter than their expected run time. The daily budget covers the overnight run with headroom. Unattended jobs have a source channel, so budget notices reach you. You've checked the log for already expired after the last restart. You know what the agent does when a tool call hangs, and you've tested it.
documents.s: A checklist before you leave it running

documents.t: Mercury can recover after a restart. Accepted jobs that were queued or interrupted are re-queued from the work ledger. That does not mean every scheduled run is replayed. Firings during downtime are skipped, and expired delayed tasks are not run. Recovery covers work that was accepted. It does not cover work that never reached the ledger.

Scheduler reliability tells you a job ran. It doesn't tell you the job did the right thing. A tool that returns success with bad data, or a task that does the wrong thing correctly, passes every check above. An overnight run needs both: a schedule that fires, and a task that is correct when it does. We'll report the open tests here as we run them.

Mercury's setup wizard uses two kinds of input. The name questions use Node's readline interface: you type a line, press Enter, and get a string back. The mode menu reads individual key presses, so it can move the highlight with the arrow keys. That needs the terminal in raw mode and a keypress listener on process.stdin. Both read from the same stream, so they have to take turns. The question reader has to let go of stdin before the menu takes over.
documents.s: Two ways to read a terminal

documents.t: In October we fixed an older bug where pressing Ctrl+D during setup made the wizard exit silently. Part of that fix was to share one readline interface across all the consecutive questions, so an end-of-input during any of them would be caught and reported. Sharing the interface raised a question: when do you close it? You don't want to close and reopen it between two questions that follow each other immediately. So after each answer, the code scheduled the close for the next turn of the event loop: iface.question(prompt, (answer) => { pending = null; scheduleRelease(); // setImmediate(() => close()) resolve(answer.trim()); }); If another question came along before then, it cancelled the scheduled close and reused the interface. That's a sensible design for a sequence of questions. The problem is what happens when the next consumer isn't a question.

Here is the exact order of events after you type your agent's name: The answer resolves. A close is scheduled for the next tick. The wizard moves on and opens the arrow-key menu. The menu puts the terminal in raw mode, calls stdin.resume(), and attaches its key listener. The next tick arrives and the scheduled close runs. readline's close() pauses its input stream, which is process.stdin. Step 3 undid step 2. The menu was waiting for key presses on a stream that was no longer flowing. Nothing else was keeping Node's event loop busy at that moment: no timers, no open sockets, no pending promises tied to I/O. When the event loop has no work left, Node exits. Cleanly. With status 0. That's why there was no error. Nothing failed. The process just ran out of things to do.

Every test we had passed, and that's the uncomfortable part. The unit tests for the question reader passed because, in isolation, it did exactly what it should. The wizard's tests mocked the menu. The binary smoke test in CI ran mercury --version, which never reaches the wizard. And anyone on the team who already had a config file never saw the first-run path at all. None of those tests had a real terminal in them, and this bug only exists when two readers share one.

The fix is one line. The menu releases the shared reader synchronously, before it takes over stdin: export async function selectWithArrowKeys(title, options, config = {}) { // Release the question reader now: its deferred close would otherwise // pause stdin after we resume it. closeAsk(); readline.emitKeypressEvents(process.stdin); // ...raw mode, resume, keypress listener } closeAsk() cancels the scheduled close and closes the interface immediately. By the time the menu calls resume(), nothing is left that could pause the stream behind its back.

The part worth copying is the test. CI now runs the compiled binary through the real first-run wizard inside a pseudo-terminal. It types a name, answers the agent name prompt, waits for the mode menu, and then checks one thing: is the process still alive? Then it presses the down arrow and Enter and expects the provider question. Run against 1.3.6, it fails at the menu. Run against 1.3.7, it passes. It runs on every pull request on Linux and macOS. There's also a regression test at the unit level that fails if a deferred release can pause the input after an explicit close.
documents.s: The test that would have caught it

documents.t: If two parts of your CLI read stdin, decide the hand-off explicitly. Don't rely on whoever closes last. "Exited with code 0" can be a bug. In Node, a process that runs out of work exits quietly. When an interactive program exits without being asked to, look for a stream that stopped flowing. Test interactive paths with a real terminal. Mocks hide the exact class of bug where two components step on each other. A pseudo-terminal test is maybe forty lines of Python and it's the only thing that would have caught this. We're sorry to everyone whose first impression of Mercury was a menu that vanished. If you bounced off it, the current release gets you through setup, and we'd love for you to try again.

The first thing I did was take the renderer out of the argument. I wrote a benchmark that mounts the real terminal UI in a virtual terminal, loads a 100-message conversation and a 14-bot roster, and types 60 characters, timing each one from key press to the frame that shows it. The median was about 3 ms per keystroke. The worst was around 20 ms. Each frame wrote roughly 74 bytes to the terminal. Then I ran it again with a bot streaming its reasoning into the UI a hundred times a second, and it barely moved: about 6 ms. That's not a renderer you can feel. Whatever was eating the latency, it wasn't drawing the screen.

So I stopped benchmarking and looked at what was actually running. There were two Mercury processes doing real work. One was the background daemon I expected. The other was the terminal session itself, and it had used about four times as much CPU as the daemon. A terminal client should use almost nothing. This one was doing a lot. The daemon's error log had the second clue: nine copies of the same Telegram error in a single day. 409 Conflict: terminated by other getUpdates request Telegram returns that when two programs poll the same bot token at once. There is no way to get it with one process.
documents.s: The process list told the story

documents.t: The launcher had a branch that looked reasonable in isolation. When you typed mercury and no background daemon was running, it did two things in a row: start the daemon, then start the agent in the foreground. autoDaemonize(); await runAgent(); The intent was to make sure Mercury kept running after you closed the terminal, while still giving you a chat right away. The effect was two complete runtimes. Both built a bot manager on the same queue. Both connected to Telegram. Both registered the same scheduled routines. And the foreground copy ran every bot turn, every tool call and every context compaction on the same thread that renders your keystrokes. For months this didn't matter much, because bots were mostly idle. Then we made them always-on. The foreground copy suddenly had real work to do, on the worst possible thread, and typing started to lag on every machine that took that path. Which was every machine, because it ran on the first mercury after any reboot. On my own laptop it was worse. An old install from npm was still registered as the login service and held the web port. Every launch failed to connect to the new daemon, decided the runtime was unhealthy, and took the "start everything" path again.
documents.s: How we ended up with two

documents.t: You can imagine a smaller fix: keep the second copy but stop it from polling Telegram, or move bot work to a worker thread. Each of those would have removed one symptom and left the actual problem in place, which is that two programs both believed they were Mercury. The fix we shipped is a rule instead: one process owns the runtime, and the terminal attaches to it. Launching mercury starts the daemon if needed and then attaches to it. The terminal never becomes a second runtime unless no daemon can run on that platform (Android under Termux is the one case). If a foreground process does start beside a live daemon, for example to open Mercury Code, it runs as a terminal for the main agent only. It doesn't register channels, doesn't create a bot manager, doesn't bind the web port, and doesn't replay scheduled work. Attaching is instant. The daemon now binds its web listener first, before channels and bots finish starting, and answers a lightweight health check with its process ID. If something else owns the port, you get one sentence saying which process it is instead of a 30-second wait followed by a pointless restart.
documents.s: Why we didn't just make it faster

documents.t: The part I'm happiest with is small. Mercury now measures its own event loop. /api/health reports the 99th-percentile and worst stall over the last ten seconds, and any stall longer than 250 ms is logged with a warning. We spent days on this bug partly because "it feels slow" isn't evidence. Now it is. If a bot turn ever does something synchronous that holds the main thread, the daemon's log will say so, with a number.

The honest version: the double runtime existed for a long time and we never noticed, because nothing measured it and the symptom only appeared once the workload changed. The tests passed because each runtime, on its own, worked. So the fix came with a few guards that would have caught it: A contract test asserts the launcher never starts the daemon and then a second runtime. The login service is checked against the running install on every launch and re-pointed if it drifted. Merges now wait for the entire CI run, not just the checks that happen to have reported so far. If you're building something that runs in the background and has a terminal front end, the takeaway is the same one we learned: decide which process is the program, and make everything else a client. It's much easier than working out, later, which of two programs is the real one.
documents.s: What we got wrong, and what we changed

documents.t: Mercury runs anywhere Node.js 22+ runs, plus everywhere a single binary can live — including phones via Termux.

macOS — curl | sh installer, Homebrew-style PATH setup, Apple Silicon & Intel binaries. Linux — works on any glibc distro; static x64/arm64 binaries. Windows — PowerShell installer, native .exe, optional WSL path. Termux & lightweight devices — Android (Termux), iSH, Alpine containers, Raspberry Pi. Cloud Instance — hosted Mercury Code via Atomic Bot. No install needed.
Every platform supports two routes — pick whichever fits.

A one-line installer downloads the latest pre-built binary, verifies its SHA-256, and puts it on your PATH. # macOS / Linux curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh # Windows irm https://mercuryagent.sh/install.ps1 | iex The installer: Detects your OS and CPU architecture (macOS arm64/x64, Linux x64/arm64, Windows x64). Resolves the latest GitHub release. Verifies the SHA-256 checksum against checksums.txt. Installs to ~/.mercury/bin/mercury (or %USERPROFILE%\.mercury\bin\mercury.exe) and updates your shell PATH. Environment variables​ Variable Default Purpose MERCURY_VERSION latest Pin to a specific version, e.g. MERCURY_VERSION=1.1.9 MERCURY_INSTALL $HOME/.mercury Install prefix (binary lands at $MERCURY_INSTALL/bin/mercury) MERCURY_NO_PATH (unset) Set to 1 to skip modifying your shell rc / user PATH

If you already have Node.js, the npm route is the simplest: npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent Other package managers: bun add -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent pnpm add -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent yarn global add @cosmicstack/mercury-agent Or run without installing: npx @cosmicstack/mercury-agent

Mercury includes a built-in upgrade command for npm installs: mercury upgrade It stops the daemon if running, removes the old package to avoid ENOTEMPTY, installs the latest version, and reports the version diff. Binary installs mercury upgrade is npm-aware. If you installed via the shell installer, re-run it to get the latest binary: curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh
After installation, run the doctor or edit your config: mercury doctor # ~/.mercury/mercury.yaml web: enabled: true The dashboard will be available at http://127.0.0.1:6174 when Mercury is running.

Mercury skills are Markdown-based extensions (SKILL.md files) that teach the agent how to do a specific task. The registry at skills.mercuryagent.sh hosts 126+ community-contributed skills across 23 categories, and Mercury can install them from four surfaces — they all share the same install path under the hood. Review before you ship. Skills run with elevated permissions when invoked. Open the registry page (mercury skills view <id> --web) and read the SKILL.md body before installing. For the file format, frontmatter spec, and runtime behavior, see Reference → Skills.

Surface Best for Entry point CLI subcommand (mercury skills …) Scripting, batch installs, JSON output mercury skills install <id> In-chat slash command (/skills …) Quick browse while chatting with the agent /skills search <q> Web dashboard Visual browse + activate/deactivate toggle http://127.0.0.1:6174/skills Telegram bot Browse and install while away from the machine /skills install <id> (admin-only) All four hit the same SkillStore.install(id) code path, write to the same ~/.mercury/skills/<category>/<slug>/SKILL.md location, and update the same ~/.mercury/skills/.index.json.
The fastest surface, available before or after starting the agent. No browser required.

mercury skills info # registry stats + reachability mercury skills categories # all 23 categories mercury skills browse finance-legal # paginated list mercury skills browse --page 2 --limit 20 mercury skills search "contract review" # full-text search mercury skills search --limit 3 prompt

mercury skills view finance-legal/contract-review mercury skills view finance-legal/contract-review --web # opens registry page mercury skills view finance-legal/contract-review --raw # prints raw SKILL.md

# From the registry mercury skills install finance-legal/contract-review mercury skills install ai-ml/prompt-engineering finance-legal/contract-review # batch mercury skills install finance-legal/contract-review --force # reinstall same version # From a local file or arbitrary URL mercury skills install --from ./SKILL.md mercury skills install --from https://example.com/my-skill.md # Update mercury skills update # all installed mercury skills update finance-legal/contract-review # just one # Remove mercury skills remove finance-legal/contract-review # Observability mercury skills list # what's installed locally mercury skills doctor # install root + registry + cache

Flag Purpose --json Machine-readable output (useful for scripting / piping). --registry <url> Use a different registry; also accepts MERCURY_SKILLS_REGISTRY. -q, --quiet Suppress progress output. -y, --yes Skip interactive confirmations. Environment variable Purpose MERCURY_SKILLS_REGISTRY Default registry URL (overridden by --registry). MERCURY_SKILLS_INSTALL_ROOT Alternate install root (defaults to ~/.mercury/skills).

Available in every channel — the CLI TUI, the web dashboard chat, and Telegram (subject to the Telegram-specific gating below). The slash command list autocompletes when you type /skills and press Tab in the CLI. /skills # list installed skills /skills search <query> # top 5 registry matches with URLs /skills view <id> # title, version, description, registry URL /skills install <id> # install from the registry /skills install <url> # install raw SKILL.md from a URL /skills remove <id> # uninstall /skills help # subcommand list Every search hit and every view response prints the https://skills.mercuryagent.sh/skills/<id> URL so you can review on the web before installing. Examples in a real chat session: > /skills search contract 🔍 Searching the registry for "contract"… Top 3 matches for "contract": • `finance-legal/contract-review` (v1.0.0) Review contracts and surface risky clauses. https://skills.mercuryagent.sh/skills/finance-legal/contract-review • `finance-legal/saas-agreement` (v0.2.1) … > /skills install finance-legal/contract-review 📦 Installing `finance-legal/contract-review` from the registry… ✅ Installed `finance-legal/contract-review` (v1.0.0) 🔗 https://skills.mercuryagent.sh/skills/finance-legal/contract-review Installs run without a confirmation prompt — same as the existing in-chat URL-install behavior. The view step (or the registry URL printed in search results) is where you should review before committing.

The Skills page in the web dashboard has two installers stacked in one card: Install from registry — paste a category/slug id and click Install. The toast reports the install status (installed, updated, reinstalled, already-installed) and the version. Install from URL — paste a URL pointing to a raw SKILL.md. Mercury fetches it, validates the frontmatter, and saves it to disk. The page header has a Browse skills.mercuryagent.sh link that opens the registry in a new tab. Each installed skill card has: A status badge (active / inactive). A toggle to activate or deactivate without deleting. A trash button to delete (with confirmation dialog). The dashboard talks to these endpoints: GET /api/skills # list installed with active state POST /api/skills/install # { url } — fetch and install from a URL POST /api/skills/install-from-registry # { id, force? } — install by registry id POST /api/skills/:name/activate POST /api/skills/:name/deactivate DELETE /api/skills/:name

Same subcommand surface as in-chat, with one extra rule: list, search, view are available to every approved user. install and remove are admin-only (same gate as /unpair). /skills # list installed /skills search <query> # registry search /skills view <id> # details + URL /skills install <id> # admin only /skills remove <id> # admin only /skills help The bot includes the https://skills.mercuryagent.sh/skills/<id> URL in every search result and every view response, so non-admin members can review a skill on a browser and then ask an admin to install it. /skills is registered in the Telegram command menu (between /spotify and /unpair), so it appears in autocomplete next to all the other bot commands.

SkillStore.install(id) calls GET /api/skills/<id> for the JSON detail, short-circuits with 'already-installed' if the local index already has the same version (unless --force), reconstructs the canonical SKILL.md from the JSON frontmatter + body fields, atomically writes it to ~/.mercury/skills/<category>/<slug>/SKILL.md (tmp file + rename), verification-reads the file back, then updates ~/.mercury/skills/.index.json. If either write fails, both the file and the index are rolled back so they never disagree. Skill ids must match ^[a-z0-9-]+/[a-z0-9-]+$ — that's the path-traversal guard. The agent picks up newly installed skills on its next discovery scan (next agent boot or /skills view in the dashboard).

Symptom Fix Invalid skill id The id must be <category>/<slug>, lowercase, hyphen-separated. Don't include the full URL. Registry 404 The id doesn't exist on the registry. Run mercury skills search <q> to find the right id. Registry timeout / unreachable Run mercury skills doctor to confirm reachability and cache state. Pass --registry or set MERCURY_SKILLS_REGISTRY if you self-host. Install succeeded but the agent doesn't see the new skill The skill loader scans on boot. Restart Mercury or open the dashboard's Skills page (it triggers a re-scan). Post-install verification failed The disk write didn't round-trip. Usually disk-full or a permission issue under ~/.mercury/skills/. The CLI rolls back automatically.

Mercury Cloud is a hosted backend that turns a local Mercury install into a remotely managed, always-on agent. Pair once from the terminal, and Mercury maintains a persistent WebSocket to the cloud — no port forwarding, no reverse proxy, no certificate management.

mercury cloud connect This opens a browser-based pairing URL. Once paired, Mercury saves your credentials and starts a background daemon that keeps the Cloud WebSocket alive even after you exit the terminal.

Pair — mercury cloud connect opens a browser URL. Poll-based completion with structured failure codes (e.g. agent capacity reached). Authenticate — Mercury receives a JWT (short-lived), a refresh token (single-use), and an agent API key (long-lived). Connect — A background daemon maintains a persistent WSS connection to wss://backend.mercuryagent.sh/ws with 30-second heartbeats and automatic reconnect. Stay online — The daemon keeps the WebSocket alive even after you close the terminal. The agent API key enables headless self-recovery without browser re-pairing.

Mercury Cloud uses a three-tier token strategy: Token Lifetime Purpose JWT Short-lived API and WebSocket auth. Auto-refreshed before expiry. Refresh token Single-use Rotated on every refresh. Used to get a new JWT. Agent API key Long-lived Headless self-recovery. Never expires. If the JWT expires, Mercury tries the refresh token. If the refresh token is also dead, Mercury redeems the agent API key to get fresh tokens — no browser re-pairing needed. This means a server or Termux deployment stays online indefinitely.

Mercury Cloud agents can search a shared memory pool — cross-agent context that lives in the cloud. After local Second Brain retrieval, the agent calls searchPool() to fetch additional context from other agents in your fleet. Results are cached locally for 5 minutes per query.
Manage your agent from cloud.mercuryagent.sh — send messages, install skills, view memory, and monitor status. The dashboard communicates with your local agent over the Cloud WebSocket.

Mercury Cloud offers multiple models. At pairing time, Mercury fetches the available models and prompts you to choose: Available models: 1. Mercury Flash (mercury-flash) 2. Mercury Pro (mercury-pro) ... Choose a model [1-N, Enter for 1]: Switch models later with /cloud use <model-id> or mercury doctor.

Command Description mercury cloud connect Pair with Mercury Cloud via browser mercury cloud disconnect Clear Cloud credentials and stop the agent mercury cloud status Show Cloud connection status and usage mercury cloud login Refresh the JWT using the stored refresh token

Mercury Cloud config is stored in mercury.yaml under the cloud section: cloud: enabled: true apiUrl: https://backend.mercuryagent.sh wsUrl: wss://backend.mercuryagent.sh/ws agentId: your-agent-id tier: free The JWT, refresh token, and agent API key are also stored here (they auto-rotate). You don't need to manage them manually.

mercury cloud disconnect This stops the running agent, clears all Cloud credentials, switches the default provider back to your offline provider, and restarts Mercury in offline mode. The agent remains registered on the cloud dashboard — delete it there to revoke server-side credentials.
Mercury runs as a background daemon by default. Telegram and scheduled tasks keep working after you close the terminal.

mercury start Starts Mercury as a background daemon. Spawns a detached child process, writes a PID file to ~/.mercury/daemon.pid, and redirects output to ~/.mercury/daemon.log. Stale PID files are automatically cleaned up.
mercury start --foreground Runs Mercury attached to your terminal. Useful for debugging or when you want to see output directly. Shorthand: mercury start -f.
mercury up This one command does everything: installs the system service if needed, starts the background daemon, and confirms Mercury is running. If it's already running, it just shows you the PID.
mercury stop Sends SIGTERM (process.kill on Windows) to the background process and removes the PID file.
mercury restart Stops the running daemon (if any) and starts a fresh one. Useful when something isn't working right and you need a clean restart.
mercury logs Shows the last 100 lines of ~/.mercury/daemon.log.

mercury status Shows whether the daemon is running, its PID, and the log file path. Crash recovery Background mode includes a watchdog. If Mercury crashes, it restarts automatically with exponential backoff (1s, 1.25s, 1.56s...). After 10 crashes within 60 seconds, it exits to prevent crash loops. Stale PID files are auto-cleaned on startup to prevent "already running" false positives.

Background tasks use human-friendly IDs like swift-fox, calm-owl, or bright-heron instead of opaque timestamps. There are 2,304 unique combinations (48 adjectives × 48 nouns). If a collision occurs, a numeric suffix is appended.
Start with /bg <command> Inspect with /bg list and /bg <id> Cancel with /bg cancel <id> (or /bg stop <id>, /bg kill <id>) Cancel all running tasks with /bg killall (or /bg stopall)
Delegate coding with /code agent <task> or /bg: <task> Move active task to worker with /bg current Worker progress/completion is surfaced in the shared background task board (/bg list)

Background tasks are persisted to disk and survive daemon restarts. Running tasks that were interrupted by a restart are marked as failed. These workers are designed to keep Mercury responsive while long-running work continues.

macOS Linux Windows mercury service install creates a LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cosmicstack.mercury.plist. Auto-start: Loads on login via launchctl load Crash recovery: KeepAlive SuccessfulExit = false restarts on crash No sudo needed: User-level LaunchAgent, not system daemon Logs: ~/.mercury/daemon.log and ~/.mercury/daemon-error.log Manual management​ launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cosmicstack.mercury.plist launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cosmicstack.mercury.plist mercury service install creates a systemd user unit at ~/.config/systemd/user/mercury.service. Mercury can be built from source two ways: Standard build — produces the regular ESM bundle in dist/, the same artifact published to npm. Good for local development, contributions, and npm link. Standalone executable — produces a single self-contained binary that embeds the JS runtime and the entire Mercury bundle. End-users do not need Node.js installed.
Node.js ≥ 20 — required for the build toolchain. Bun ≥ 1.3 — only needed if you're building standalone binaries. Install Bun: curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash

git clone https://github.com/cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent.git cd mercury-agent npm install npm run build # tsup + post-build (UI, static assets, wasm) npm start # runs node dist/index.js To use your local build as the global mercury command: npm link mercury --help
Mercury uses bun build --compile to embed the entire bundle into a single platform-native binary. The resulting file runs on machines with no Node.js, no Bun, and no dependencies installed.
npm install npm run build:bin # builds the binary for your current OS/arch ./release/v1.1.9/mercury-macos-arm64 --help

Command Targets Behavior on existing build npm run build:bin host only skip if already built npm run build:bin:all all 5 platforms skip per-target npm run build:bin:force host only overwrite npm run build:bin:all:force all 5 platforms overwrite Supported targets for --all: macOS arm64 (Apple Silicon) macOS x64 (Intel) Linux x64 Linux arm64 Windows x64

The build script reads the version from package.json and writes binaries into a versioned subfolder. Older builds are never overwritten — you can keep many versions side-by-side. release/ ├── latest → symlink to the most-recent version ├── v1.1.9/ │ ├── mercury-macos-arm64 │ ├── mercury-macos-x64 │ ├── mercury-linux-x64 │ ├── mercury-linux-arm64 │ ├── mercury-win-x64.exe │ └── checksums.txt (SHA-256 for every binary in the folder) └── v1.2.0/ └── ... Bump version in package.json before building and the script automatically creates a new folder. If a binary for the current version+target already exists, the script skips it (printing ↷ skip (already built)) unless you pass --force. Verify integrity with the generated checksums: cd release/v1.1.9 shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt # mercury-macos-arm64: OK

Bun ships its own runtime per target, so you can build all five platforms from any one host (e.g. produce a Windows .exe from your Mac): npm run build:bin:all Native node modules can't cross-compile, but Mercury's only native dep (better-sqlite3) is optional — at runtime the binary falls back to sql.js (pure JS + wasm). Cross-compiled binaries are fully functional.

Unsigned binaries trigger Gatekeeper on first launch. For local use, right-click → Open once and macOS will remember the choice. For distribution: codesign --sign "Developer ID Application: Your Name" release/v1.1.9/mercury-macos-arm64 xcrun notarytool submit release/v1.1.9/mercury-macos-arm64 --apple-id ... --wait Why Bun and not pkg / Node SEA? Mercury's dependency graph includes ESM modules with top-level await (ink, yoga-layout). Both pkg and Node.js Single Executable Applications require CommonJS entry points and can't transform top-level await. Bun runs ESM natively and embeds its own runtime, so it sidesteps the whole problem.

bun: command not found — install Bun with curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash, then either restart your shell or use the explicit path ~/.bun/bin/bun. ERROR: dist/index.js not found — the bin script depends on the standard build. The build:bin npm script chains both; if you ran the bin script directly, prefix with npm run build. Binary silently exits with code 0 — usually means the package.json version lookup failed. The build pipeline injects the version at compile time via tsup --define. If you've modified the entry file, make sure the pkgVersion fallback path remains intact (see src/index.ts). Stale release/latest symlink — re-running any build:bin command repairs the symlink to point at the current package.json version.

Mercury runs on any modern Linux distro with glibc ≥ 2.31 (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, Fedora 34+, Arch, etc.) on x86_64 or arm64.

curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh The installer picks the right binary for your CPU, verifies the SHA-256 checksum, places it at ~/.mercury/bin/mercury, and adds that directory to your shell PATH (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or ~/.config/fish/config.fish). After install: exec $SHELL -l mercury --version :::note Older x86-64 CPUs The default Linux x64 build uses AVX2. On a CPU without it (Intel before 2013, some VMs) the installer picks the baseline build automatically — from /proc/cpuinfo, or by switching after an Illegal instruction crash. To force it: MERCURY_ASSET=mercury-linux-x64-baseline curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh. :::
npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent Requires Node.js 22+. Recommended via nvm so you avoid sudo for global packages.

Mercury runs on Android via Termux, giving you a real coding agent in your pocket. It also works in other minimal environments like iSH (iOS), Alpine containers, and Raspberry Pi.

Android 7.0+ Termux installed from F-Droid or GitHub Releases (the Play Store build is unmaintained — do not use it) ~500 MB free storage for Node.js, Mercury, and native module compilation Network access

Termux is the recommended path on Android because the prebuilt Linux binaries target glibc, while Termux uses bionic libc. Use the npm route: pkg update && pkg upgrade -y pkg install nodejs-lts git python make clang pkg-config -y npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent mercury nodejs-lts provides Node 22+ (required since 1.3.1) and npm. Python, Make, Clang, and pkg-config are required when npm needs to build native dependencies such as better-sqlite3 for Android's bionic libc. Do not use Mercury's standalone Linux binary on Termux.

Let Mercury read/write files in your Android storage: termux-setup-storage # grants ~/storage/ symlinks: ~/storage/shared, ~/storage/downloads, etc. Now you can point Mercury at projects in ~/storage/shared/Projects/....

Android may stop Termux processes when the app is swiped away or the device sleeps. For the best available background behavior: Install Termux:API and Termux:Boot from the same source as Termux (F-Droid or GitHub), then install the API commands: pkg install termux-api termux-wake-lock Disable battery optimization for Termux in Settings → Apps → Termux → Battery. Start Mercury with its supported daemon command: mercury start Termux does not run systemd, so mercury service install is intentionally unsupported. To request startup after reboot, create ~/.termux/boot/start-mercury: mkdir -p ~/.termux/boot cat > ~/.termux/boot/start-mercury <<'EOF' #!/data/data/com.termux/files/usr/bin/sh termux-wake-lock mercury start EOF chmod +x ~/.termux/boot/start-mercury Termux:Boot only runs after the user has opened its app once, and Android/OEM background restrictions can still stop Mercury. A wakelock reduces suspension but increases battery use; release it with termux-wake-unlock when Mercury is stopped. This setup cannot guarantee server-like 24/7 availability. See Daemon Mode for mercury start, mercury status, and mercury stop details.
documents.s: Keep Mercury running in the background

documents.t: A common Termux setup: run Mercury's Telegram integration on your phone so you can chat with it from any device. mercury doctor # enable Telegram, paste bot token mercury start

No prebuilt binary — must use npm. The standalone installer (install.sh) won't work on Termux because of glibc/bionic differences. No system service manager — systemd service install/status/uninstall is unavailable. Use Mercury's daemon commands and optionally Termux:Boot. No guaranteed background uptime — wakelocks and Termux:Boot cannot override every Android or OEM process-killing policy. TUI rendering — Mercury's interface assumes a wide terminal. Rotate landscape or pair Termux with an external keyboard for the best experience. Background limits — Aggressive OEMs (Xiaomi, Oppo, Huawei) need extra battery-optimization tweaks beyond the standard Android settings. Storage permission — Required for accessing project files outside $HOME.
mercury upgrade …or: npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent@latest

iSH runs an Alpine Linux user-space on iOS. Mercury works there via npm: apk add nodejs npm npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent mercury Performance is limited — iSH emulates x86 via usermode, so expect slow startup. Best used for read-only / chat-style sessions.

Alpine uses musl libc, so the standalone Linux binary won't load. Use npm: apk add --no-cache nodejs npm git npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent This applies to Docker images based on alpine:* as well.

64-bit Pi OS (Pi 3/4/5): the standard Linux installer works — pulls mercury-linux-arm64. 32-bit Pi OS or armv6 (Pi Zero, Pi 1): no prebuilt binary; install via npm: curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_20.x | sudo -E bash - sudo apt install -y nodejs npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent

If your platform isn't listed and the binary doesn't run (Exec format error, missing libc), the npm route always works as long as Node.js 20+ is available. If Node isn't packaged for your OS, see Build From Source.
